# T112 — spend the card on training, not on discovering something does not work
## Why this exists

Operator, 2026-09-18: "I want a 100% utilisation of the 4090 today (I want it to be a meaningful increase on the LB rank) … make extensive plans and reverify the flow such that this does[n't] waste my resources tomorrow." And, mid-session: "2.5D CoAtNet at 224 — this guy is at 0.95."
The card arrives the morning of 2026-09-19.
The failure this task exists to prevent is not "we trained the wrong thing" — it is "we trained the right thing and could not score it."
## THE FINDING THAT WOULD HAVE COST THE DAY

src/coat_model.py's CoatMIL and the adopted notebook's RaptorClassifier are mathematically identical: same LayerNorm, same Sequential(Linear(F,256), Tanh, Dropout, Linear(256,12)), same clsW/clsb, same einsum('bkn,bkf->bnf'), backbones built with the same num_classes=0, in_chans=3, global_pool='avg'.
They are not the same state dict:
ours
theirs
head.norm.weight · head.att.0.weight · head.clsW · head.clsb
norm.weight · att.0.weight · clsW · clsb
Their loader is model.load_state_dict(ck['model'], strict=True).
Every checkpoint we have ever trained for this arm would have been REFUSED by the pipeline that scores it — and the refusal would have landed at the end of an eight-hour Kaggle run, not at the start.

Fixed and proven today, offline, on CPU (src/coat_export.py): the converted state dict loads at strict=True with zero missing and zero unexpected keys, and on identical weights and an identical bag the two forwards agree to max |Δ| = 0.000e+00 — bit-identical.
The reference class is extracted from the notebook, never retyped, so if their class changes the test fails instead of passing against a stale copy.

224 is 3.01× cheaper than 384 and 2.50× cheaper than 352 — and it is a legal size (224 = 32 × 7).
A correction this task had to make about its own claim. "336 is illegal" is true of res — the size the model sees — and false of img, the decode size.
Cell 47 groups arms by (img, slots, span, k_eval), decodes each group's studies once, and then resizes per arm to res inside eval_windows.
Their own dominant arm, maxspan-v5, decodes at img 336 — 32 × 10.5 — and is perfectly legal because only res reaches the backbone.
Two defects followed from conflating the two, both caught by a control and both fixed before anything was pushed:
The builder defaulted img to our resolution.
At 224 that opens a fourth decode group — one more full pass over the test set, against T105's measured 429–434 min and a registered 495-min cap, i.e. about 60 minutes of margin.
assert_decode_group_preserved() now refuses any img/k_eval that does not match the member being replaced.
The multiple-of-32 rule guarded img instead of res, so the builder refused to render a maxspan-v5 swap at all, with a message that was confidently wrong about why.

The registered configuration is therefore res = ours, img/slots/span/k_eval = the replaced member's. Our arm costs GPU passes only, never another decode, and the kernel's own [plan] N arms over M volume recipe(s) line must still report 3 — which is now asserted.
The operator's intel says a competitor is at 0.95 with a 2.5D CoAtNet at 224, which is our framing: our corpus is (N, 44, 336, 336) and our window is already three consecutive slices as RGB.
That intel is operator-supplied and unverified by us;
it is a reason to prefer 224, not a measurement.
T065 B1's "224 px is closed" does NOT bind here. It was registered against arm C / tf_efficientnet_b2 at 320, a different architecture on a different input path.
A pre-registered rule binds to its written scope.
4090 projection, labelled as a projection: the public trainer's author documents ~3.0 h for the full 384/bs8 16-epoch recipe on one 4090;
our laptop does 384/bs2 in 10.6 h, so the card is ~3.5×.
Applied to 224 that is ~1.0 h per 16-epoch fold.
scripts/t112/bringup_4090.sh measures it for real in 30 seconds before a single hour is committed — nothing downstream depends on the projection being right.
## THE DEFECT THAT WOULD HAVE BEEN RECORDED AS A RESULT
Their eval_windows ends:
and NORM = "imagenet" for every arm.
src/coat_data.py divided by 255 and stopped. Measured 2026-09-18: their inputs carry ~4.48× our standard deviation and a −0.24 mean shift.
A model fitted on [0, 1] and scored on that is being shown a different distribution.

What makes this the dangerous kind of defect rather than the loud kind: the kernel runs clean, the VOID banner prints because the arm really did run, and the score comes back low — which this task's own registered rule reads as "≤ 0.934 → REJECT.
Our arm is worse." We would have entered a resolved negative about our own architecture into the permanent record on the strength of a normalisation mismatch.
That is worse than a wasted day;
a wasted day can be repeated.
Two fixes, both pre-registered here before any score exists:
Tonight's fold stays submittable. The arm carries its own "norm": "none" in the ARMS entry and the call site becomes norm=arm.get("norm", NORM).
The other three arms keep "imagenet" and are unchanged in behaviour — asserted: exactly 1 of 4 entries declares a normalisation.
Still one cell, because the call site lives in cell 47 too.
The VOID banner names the normalisation, so the log proves which distribution the arm was scored under.
src/coat_train.py --norm {none,imagenet}, recorded in RECIPE and printed in the run header.
Default stays none so tonight's fold reproduces exactly;
stored_recipe() defaults the field for checkpoints written before it existed, so --resume cannot refuse a run that is the same recipe.

And a prediction worth registering: --norm imagenet should be BETTER, not merely consistent. sw_in12k_ft_in1k was pretrained under ImageNet normalisation, so tonight's gold-58 0.8848 was reached despite feeding the frozen features an out-of-distribution input. Tomorrow's first 4090 fold is therefore --norm imagenet, one variable against tonight's, and if it does not beat 0.8848 on gold-58 that is a recorded miss.
## THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES EVERYTHING: scoring, not training
Submit-to-COMPLETE is 429–434 minutes — 7 h 09 m to 7 h 14 m (T105, measured against an HTTP Date header, not this machine's RTC).
Five submissions a day;
T057 rule 5 caps 3 structurally distinct.
So the day has at most two sequential read-then-act cycles:
push
scores
Training is no longer the bottleneck.
Scoring is. At ~1 h/fold the card can produce seven arms tomorrow and we can read at most two.
A plan that trains seven and scores two has not achieved 100% utilisation — it has achieved 30% and a pile of unscored checkpoints.
The consequence, and it is the whole plan: the 08:00 submission must be built from a checkpoint that already exists at 08:00.
The card cannot produce it — it will still be in its box.
So:
> ### The laptop buys the first submission slot.
The 4090 buys the second, and the family.
## The schedule, pre-registered
Tonight (laptop, ~3.6 h, requires operator approval — it is a GPU spend):

- One fold, --res 224 --bs 4 --accum 2 --epochs 16 (effective batch 8, the recipe's own), under scripts/gpu_queue.sh so the idle+sleep inhibitor is held (T067: --what=idle alone does not stop gsd-power). 5.55 GiB of 7.62 — it fits without chunking, and it is inside the one-fold-then-cool-down ruling at 3.6 h, unlike the 8.8 h 352 fold.
- It produces the morning's gold-58 reading before any 4090 hour is spent.

Why --bs 4 --accum 2 and not --bs 2 --accum 4. Both give effective batch 8, and T091 measured on b2 why that is not the same thing: --accum 4 at micro-batch 2 scored 0.887 — WRONG, resolved, because "effective batch 8 at BN batch 2 is NOT a test of true batch 8".
BatchNorm normalises over the micro-batch, and coatnet_rmlp_2 carries 25 BatchNorm2d layers.
The public recipe is true bs 8 on a 24 GB card, so the larger micro-batch is the one closer to the recipe we are reproducing, not further from it.
At 224 the laptop affords micro-batch 4 (5.55 GiB of 7.62) where at 352 it could only afford 2 — which is a second, independent reason 224 is the right lane tonight.

## Decision rules — fixed now, before any number exists

BROKEN → do not submit, debug. gold-58 < 0.85 at full fidelity — defined here, on review, as measured under the KERNEL's resample chain and window count (condition B of scripts/t112/resample_delta.py: 336 → 384 → 224, k_eval 42), not the trainer's.
"Full fidelity" was undefined when this was written, and the difference between the two chains is exactly what D4 measures.
The published arm reads 0.9054–0.9213 on gold-58 — four irreconcilable public figures for that checkpoint, with T044's rule that "no single one may be quoted as the target";
the range T107/T111 carried, 0.9128–0.9213, silently dropped the lowest.
Our teacher is 0.8976.
VOID → not submitted. The kernel log must contain [t112] OUR ARM IS IN THE STAGE: {'file': …, 'replaced': 'native384-v8', 'w': 0.2}.
If that line is absent the arm did not swap and the run scores the unchanged 0.941 parent — a null that is not a null.
scripts/t112/build_t112_kernel.py raises rather than rendering a no-op patch, and the render is asserted to differ from T105's kernel in exactly one cell.
SUBMISSION 1, read against S = 0.941 at ±0.007 (T111's registered band, not renegotiated):
- ≥ 0.948 → ADOPT. Our arm is better than theirs in the stage.
Submission 2 becomes the dominant-member swap (maxspan-v5, w 0.55 + reverse 0.15 = 0.70).
- ≤ 0.934 → REJECT. Our arm is worse.
Submission 2 is not spent chasing it;
the day records a resolved negative, which is a result.
- between → UNRESOLVED. Submission 2 is the same swap trained longer on the 4090 (more epochs or SWA), one variable, and no weight sweep (T057 rule 6).
Prediction, written before the score exists: 0.938–0.946. Recorded so it can be a miss.

T106 is the same experiment at the same stage weight, and it moved 0.000. ADOPT asks a ~7%-weight member substitution for +0.007 on a leaderboard where this project's last four structural changes moved 0.000, 0.000, −0.001 and −0.002.
And the prediction above, 0.938–0.946, lies almost entirely inside the UNRESOLVED band, 0.934–0.948 — the plan predicted the reading that means "no conclusion".
That is an honest prediction and a self-defeating experiment in the same sentence.
The local instrument already leans the same way. Our arm reads gold-58 0.8848;
the member it replaces reads 0.9054–0.9213 on the same 58 studies.
That is a −0.02 to −0.04 gap — at the edge of the ±0.036 band, so not resolved, but against us in all four of the published readings.
Our student is still below its own teacher (0.8848 vs 0.8976), which is the b2 era's defect in a new architecture, not yet cured by it.

The alternative review raised, recorded here as a trade rather than settled by ordering: swapping maxspan-v5 + its reverse view puts our arm at 0.70 of the stage ≈ 25% of the final blend — 3.5× the signal — but moves the framing to _SLOTS64 and span 0.02–0.98, where our fold (trained on _SLOTS44) has never been;
it would no longer be one variable.
Which slot, and whether to spend a submission on this arm at all, is the operator's call.
## What +0.009 actually requires, stated honestly
The operator wants a meaningful rank move — 0.941 → 0.950 is rank ~25, 0.952 is rank 20.
The evidence does not support expecting that from one day, and this task will not pretend it does:
what we tried
what it moved
T106 — our best single model added to the stack at w = 0.2
T108 — two registered presets
T110 — dropping the entire transformer branch
T105 — adopting someone else's notebook wholesale
Every gain this project has recorded above 0.928 came from adopting, not from tuning.

The one lever with real headroom left is exactly this task's: a better CoAtNet arm than theirs, because our teacher is ours and it is good. ~~A realistic good day is~~ (struck on review: "realistic" was the word the four rows directly above argue against) The best case is clearing 0.948 and resolving ADOPT — which would be the first time our own modelling moved the standing at all.
0.950 is the stretch, not the plan.

Paired Δ (ours − theirs) = −0.0277, 95% CI [−0.0483, −0.0076] → RESOLVED, ours is BEHIND.
Their reading agrees with an independent measurement: T071 scored the same checkpoint on the same 58 at 0.9002–0.9187 (outputs/t071/fidelity.txt), against its own stored 0.9214.
It is held-out, not in-sample: T071 verified "their gold set IS our 58", and the public trainer holds out the real-labelled studies (outputs/t107/train_knee_public.py:33).
What this changes, before any score exists: the registered swap (submission 1) is withdrawn.
An arm that is resolved-behind the member it replaces is expected to lower the stack at any weight — at ~7% effective weight, too little to see;
at the 25% maxspan-v5 slot, a real drop.
This is a decision made on a resolved local instrument before any leaderboard read, so T057 rule 6 (no re-picking after a score) is not engaged.
Stated limits: the comparison is against v5, not v8 (the member the registered swap replaces) — v8 is not on disk. v5 was deployed on 64 slots with 62 windows;
it is scored here with 42 windows over the corpus's 44 slices.
Neither limit favours us: T071's denser-slice rung read v5 higher (0.9187), not lower.

The instrument this leaves behind is the real deliverable. Every 4090 run can now be read as a paired delta against v5 with a CI of roughly ±0.02 — against gold-58's absolute ±0.036, the first local instrument in this project that can rank two arms of this architecture.
The bar for any future submission of our arm: paired Δ vs v5 whose 95% CI lower bound is ≥ 0.
## What adversarial review found, and what it changed
A critic pass over this work REJECTED it, and was right to.
Recorded because the finding is the same shape as the one this task was created for.

BLOCKER — the kernel never attached our dataset. render() copies T108's kernel-metadata.json, and T108's two kernels are the only recent family that ship no checkpoint of ours — so dataset_sources was inherited verbatim with our dataset absent, and find_weight_file("ours_coat_t112.pt") would have raised.

That call sits outside the per-study try/except, and the Raptor arm is Stage 4, the last stage — the DINO, A5 and RadImageNet stages all finish first, so the exception arrives with roughly six of the run's seven hours spent, on a kernel that then cannot be submitted at all.

The exact twin of the strict=True defect, one layer out, and I had missed it while being pleased about the first one. Fixed: add_dataset_source() attaches it, render() asserts it against the file it wrote, and the suite now checks the invariant that ties the halves — the pushed metadata names the dataset holding the file the rendered ARMS entry asks for.
Its control failed first, on an empty slug that satisfied the assertion while attaching nothing.

BLOCKER — make dryrun did not pass, and "9/9" was read off a crashed run. My own two previous fixes broke it: train_norm made stage 4's key assertion false, and the decode-group guard refused the img=224 the script still passed.
It printed nine PASS lines and then a traceback.

A report that passes for the wrong reason is the same defect as a check that does, one level up. Fixed, and the stage count is now gated like the smoke suite: EXPECTED_STAGES is asserted, a crash is recorded as a failed stage, and the gate immediately caught my own miscount (13 ran, 12 declared).
--res was an input where it should have been an assertion. Their load_model reads ck['res'];
the ARMS entry's is only a fallback.
--res 352 on a 224 checkpoint rendered a fully consistent kernel, converted cleanly, passed every control, and would have scored the wrong thing.
It is now checked against the checkpoint's own recipe.
Also fixed: push_arm.py used one kaggle binary to decide whether the dataset existed and a different one to act.

## T112 — the join that would have cost the 4090's first day (2026-09-18)
The card arrives 2026-09-19.
The failure worth preventing was never "we trained the wrong thing" — it was "we trained the right thing and could not score it."

CoatMIL and the adopted notebook's RaptorClassifier are mathematically identical — same LayerNorm, same Sequential(Linear(F,256), Tanh, Dropout, Linear(256,12)), same clsW/clsb, same einsum('bkn,bkf->bnf'), backbones built with the same num_classes=0, in_chans=3, global_pool='avg'.
They are not the same state dict: ours nests the head under head., theirs holds it as direct attributes, and their loader is load_state_dict(ck['model'], strict=True).
Every checkpoint this project has trained for the adopted arm would have been REFUSED by the pipeline that scores it — and the refusal lands at the end of an eight-hour Kaggle run, not at the start.
Eight characters of key prefix against a day of a card we do not yet own.

src/coat_export.py renames them and writes the three fields load_model() actually reads (model, arch, res — res is the resolution our arm is evaluated at, so a 224 arm shipped without it would be scored at their 384).

Verified offline on CPU: zero missing, zero unexpected, and the two forwards agree to max |Δ| = 0.000e+00 — bit-identical. The reference class is extracted from the notebook, never retyped, so a change on their side fails the test instead of passing against a stale copy.

Also built and verified today: scripts/t112/build_t112_kernel.py (the swap, in T110's idiom — every edit raises rather than no-opping, exactly one cell differs from T105's kernel, the replaced member's weight is carried so the swap stays one variable, and a banner the VOID gate greps so an absent arm fails instead of scoring the unchanged parent as a null);
scripts/t112/dry_run.py (make dryrun — the whole chain on the real corpus and the real notebook, CPU-only, 9/9 stages);
and scripts/t112/bringup_4090.sh with a 20-entry transfer manifest, including the control that proves its teacher check can fail on the leak file.
Measured, on the laptop 4070: res 224 = 15.21 ms/window at 3.36 GiB, 3.5 h for 16 epochs — 3.01× cheaper than 384, 2.50× cheaper than 352, and legal (32 × 7).
Operator intel, unverified by us: a competitor is at 0.95 with a 2.5D CoAtNet at 224, which is our framing.
T065 B1's "224 px is closed" does not bind here — it was registered against tf_efficientnet_b2 at 320.
The constraint that shapes tomorrow, and it is not the GPU. Submit-to-COMPLETE is 429–434 min, so at five a day there are at most two read-then-act cycles.
On a 4090 training stops being the bottleneck;
scoring never does.
The 08:00 submission must be built from a checkpoint that exists before the card is unboxed — which is why a 224 fold went on the laptop tonight, on operator approval.
